figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Routing across modalities. (a) For each input, the router picks one candidate from the pool based on demand, ranking candidates by value minus weighted cost. (b) On the test set, the best candidate per input (oracle) beats the best fixed candidate per benchmark by 5.4 points on average (Table 1). (c) Routing raises efficiency by $8.82\times$ on average over the reference model, at a quality loss below 0.5 points. The efficiency gain, $\eta/\eta_{B}$, compares quality per dollar (or per second of policy inference for robots) against the reference (Table 5).
figures.headline: Per-input routing lifts the oracle 5.4 points above the best fixed candidate and raises efficiency 8.82× over the reference.
citing_sentences: To support such anlyasitical framework, we first build an omni-modal trajectory matrix in which every candidate in a pool runs on the same inputs, for 25 benchmarks across text and image understanding, image, video, and speech generation, code and workplace agents, and robot manipulation, with three to seven candidates per pool and 374,401 scored runs of 452 candidate configurations (Figure 1).

abstract: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) requires a method that can understand, generate, reason, and act across diverse domains and modalities. Rather than relying on a single model to master every capability, a promising path toward AGI now is to orchestrate a heterogeneous ecosystem of specialized models, tools, and policies (candidates) into a unified AI system. At the heart of this vision lies a fundamental question: how can an AI system dynamically select and coordinate the most capable candidate for each task while balancing performance and computational cost? In this work, we present Route Anything, a unified framework for studying model and policy routing across general-purpose AI systems. We develop a unified theoretical foundation that characterizes optimal routing under quality–cost trade-offs and establishes how the information available to a router determines its attainable performance. To systematically investigate routing across diverse capabilities, we first construct an omni-modal trajectory matrix spanning 25 benchmarks across language understanding, image, video, and speech generation, coding and workplace agents, and robotic manipulation, comprising 374,401 scored runs from 452 candidate configurations. Building on this framework, we train and test different routers to investigate the potential of omni-modal model routing, the capabilities of learned routers, and the conditions under which routing improves efficiency. Our results reveal substantial opportunities for capability orchestration: per-input oracle routing outperforms the best fixed candidate by 5.4 points, and learned routers outperform it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks, by 2.1 points on video generation, and by 1.1 points on robot manipulation while using 24% less policy time. More importantly, routing raises efficiency by $8.82\times$ on average compared with the reference model, including $25.5\times$ on coding tasks and $7.1\times$ on text question answering.

sections.body: The introduction frames routing as choosing, for each input, one candidate from a pool of language models, image, video or speech generators, or robot policies. A good router is expected either to match the strongest fixed candidate at lower cost or to beat it. The authors build an omni-modal trajectory matrix in which every candidate runs on the same inputs: 25 benchmarks, three to seven candidates per pool, and 374,401 scored runs across 452 candidate configurations. They ask three questions: how much routing can gain, how well learned routers work, and when a cheaper route is good enough. Reported results include a 5.4-point gain for per-input oracle routing over the best fixed candidate, a 0.3-point gain for learned routers across 16 benchmarks, and an average efficiency gain of 8.82× over the reference.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Routing is posed as choosing one candidate per input across 25 benchmarks and 452 candidate configurations.

sections.body: A router maps an observed state to a candidate, scored by expected value minus price times expected cost. Lemma 1 gives the condition for beating a reference on efficiency, plus a separate quality floor. Theorem 2 states that at a given price, optimal routers play, in each state, a candidate maximizing value minus price times cost. Proposition 3 orders attainable value by observed information, from the best fixed candidate to the per-input oracle. Proposition 4 shows that regressing on outcomes reaches the oracle at zero price, while predicting winners can lose much of the value. Proposition 5 certifies a quality floor with a finite-sample test. Results assume finitely many states and positive costs.
sections.heading: A Router’s Value
sections.headline: The information a router observes bounds its attainable value, and its optimal form is routing at a single price.

sections.body: Table 1 pools 19,814 test inputs on which every candidate is scored, with values on a 0–100 scale. The best fixed candidate per benchmark scores 82.60 and the per-input oracle scores 87.98, a gap of 5.38 points. The gap is 0.68 for speech generation, 18.93 for video generation and 18.40 for robot manipulation. Choosing the best candidate per capability type in hindsight recovers 8% of the gap on the 18-benchmark rule-based tree, where it scores 77.89 against 77.03 for the fixed candidate and 87.44 for the oracle. Part of the within-type variation is outcome noise that no router can predict: on AA-LCR, the oracle margin of 2.4 points vanishes when each candidate is scored by its mean over three runs. Seven understanding benchmarks are excluded from the learned-router studies.
sections.heading: Can Router Beat the Best Fixed Candidate?
sections.headline: The per-input oracle scores 87.98 against 82.60 for the best fixed candidate, and most of the gap lies within task types.

sections.body: The router studies fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B on task text and output requirements. An outcome router scores each input and candidate pair with a sigmoid head and plays the highest score. A type router classifies inputs into capability types. The capability-tree router, with 157 leaves, scores 79.98 against 79.68 for the fixed candidate across 16 benchmarks, and the oracle scores 84.80. On RoboTwin, an outcome router reads three camera frames and the robot state, and scores 71.55 against 70.45 for the fixed policy, a difference of 1.10 with interval [-0.40, +2.55]. It uses 11.05 seconds of policy time per scene against 14.51. A winner-label classifier on the same robot inputs reaches 42.80. The section attributes this to latency tie-breaks that shape the winner labels. Matched comparisons show that requiring a score on every training input biases the fixed baseline downward.
sections.heading: How Well Do Learned Routers Work?
sections.headline: One learned router scores 79.98 against 79.68 for the fixed candidate across 16 benchmarks and matches it on ten.

sections.body: The section prices candidates in USD for code and text and in seconds for robot policies. On CodeRouterBench, a route that never calls the reference reaches 25.5× the reference's efficiency at a quality change of -0.44 points. On RouterBench, the efficiency gain is 7.1× at -0.40 points. For image generation, efficiency reaches 1.35× with a tolerance of 0.5 and 2.03× with a tolerance of 2. The robot outcome router reaches 1.33× with a quality change of +1.10. Certified routes hold the floor in all 200 splits on both code and text. The section also reports limits: a zero-loss floor fitted on half the probing tasks holds on test in only 12.5% of 200 splits. Retries and verifier cascades are kept only when their gains exceed the cost of the extra attempt.
sections.heading: When Is a Cheaper Route Good Enough?
sections.headline: Routing to cheaper candidates raises efficiency over the reference by 8.82× on average, at a small quality cost.

sections.body: Related work covers cascades and learned routers for language models, deferral rules, and routers that extend beyond model identity. Algorithm portfolios are named as the closest precedent, where the virtual best solver corresponds to the per-input oracle. One prior study characterizes optimal routing with a Lagrangian price tuned to a budget. This paper differs by fixing the price from a reference and a quality tolerance, and by certifying the resulting floor with a finite-sample test. It also places language models, image, video and speech generators, and robot policies on one matrix with shared inputs. The section lists value of information and feedback-driven self-repair as adjacent questions.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: The related work places routing alongside cascades, portfolios, and test-time compute, and extends them to image, video, speech, and robot outputs.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the 5.4-point gap between the per-input oracle and the best fixed candidate. It reports 0.3 points for learned routers across 16 benchmarks, with gains of 2.1 points on video generation and 1.1 points on robot manipulation, and attributes most potential gain to variation within task types. For efficiency, it reports 8.82× on average over the reference. It states that the reference and the tolerance fix the price, and that a finite-sample test certifies the floor. Three rules follow. First, compare candidates on the same inputs and measure gains against the matched best fixed candidate. Second, train routers on per-candidate outcomes and look for gains within task types. Third, fix the reference and tolerance before ranking routes, and certify the floor on independent inputs.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Routing gains come chiefly from cheaper routes that are good enough, and three rules follow for comparing and training routers.

sections.body: Appendix A proves Lemma 1 and Theorem 2, and gives the proofs for Propositions 3 and 4 together with the floor certification results. The Lemma 1 proof writes the efficiency difference as the quality change plus the reference efficiency times the saving, divided by expected cost. Appendix C reports verifier cascades: for Qwen3-Max at a threshold of 0.5, a free compiler gate gives 4.09× dollar efficiency at a 2.4-point loss. An LLM forecast can cost more than the attempt it saves. Nine released routers are evaluated as signals by capture, and router memory is tested on semi-synthetic streams, where the store reaches 135.8 score per dollar but scores 0.034 below always-Opus. The stated limits are that the theory takes the law of states as given, and that step-level routing for long-horizon tasks needs further study.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix gives proofs of the theory and extra experiments on verifiers, routing signals, and router memory, and states limitations.
